source_text: Διακόπτει γὰρ ταῖς ἑαυτοῦ χηλαῖς τῶν καρπῶν τὸ μεσαίτατον, ὡς ἂν μὴ ἐκφυέντες ἄχρηστοι πρὸς τροφὴν αὐτῷ γένοιντο. Καὶ διαψύχει τούτους, ὅταν αἴσθηται αὐτῶν διαβρόχων· καὶ οὐκ ἐν παντὶ προβάλλει καιρῷ, ἀλλ' ὅταν προαίσθηται τοῦ ἀέρος ἐν εὐδινῇ καταστάσει φυλαττομένου. Ἀμέλει οὐκ ἂν ἴδοις ὄμβρον ἐκ νεφῶν ἐπιρρυέντα παρ' ὅσον χρόνον ἐκ τῶν μυρμήκων ὁ σῖτος προβέβληται. Τίς ἐφίκηται λόγος; ποία χωρήσει ἀκοή; τίς ἐξαρκέσει χρόνος πάντα εἰπεῖν καὶ διηγήσασθαι τοῦ τεχνίτου τὰ θαύματα; Εἴπωμεν καὶ ἡμεῖς μετὰ τοῦ προφήτου, Ὡς ἐμεγαλύνθη τὰ ἔργα σου, Κύριε· πάντα ἐν σοφίᾳ ἐποίησας. Οὐ τοίνυν ἡμῖν πρὸς ἀπολογίαν αὔταρκες, τὸ μὴ γράμμασι διδαχθῆναι τὰ συμφέροντα, τῷ ἀδιδάκτῳ τῆς φύσεως νόμῳ τὴν τοῦ λυσιτελοῦντος αἵρεσιν δεξαμένοις. Οἶδας τί ποιήσεις τῷ πλησίον καλόν; Ὃ σεαυτῷ βούλει παρ' ἑτέρου γενέσθαι. Οἶδας ὅ τι ποτέ ἐστι τὸ κακόν; Ὃ οὐκ ἂν αὐτὸς παθεῖν ἕλοιο παρ' ἑτέρου. Οὐδεμία ῥιζοτομικὴ τέχνη, οὐδὲ ἐμπειρία βοτανικὴ τῶν ὠφελίμων τοῖς ἀλόγοις τὴν διδασκαλίαν ἐξεῦρεν, ἀλλὰ φυσικῶς ἕκαστον τῶν ζῴων τῆς οἰκείας ἐστὶ σωτηρίας ποριστικὸν, καὶ ἄρρητόν τινα κέκτηται τὴν πρὸς τὸ κατὰ φύσιν οἰκείωσιν. 9.4 Εἰσὶ δὲ καὶ παρ' ἡμῖν αἱ ἀρεταὶ κατὰ φύσιν, πρὸς ἃς ἡ οἰκείωσις τῆς ψυχῆς οὐκ ἐκ διδασκαλίας ἀνθρώπων, ἀλλ' ἐξ αὐτῆς τῆς φύσεως ἐνυπάρχει. Ὡς γὰρ οὐδεὶς ἡμᾶς λόγος διδάσκει τὴν νόσον μισεῖν, ἀλλ' αὐτόματον ἔχομεν τὴν πρὸς τὰ λυποῦντα διαβολήν· οὕτω καὶ τῇ ψυχῇ ἔστι τις ἀδίδακτος ἔκκλισις τοῦ κακοῦ. Κακὸν δὲ πᾶν ἀρρωστία ψυχῆς, ἡ δὲ ἀρετὴ λόγον ὑγιείας ἐπέχει. Καλῶς γὰρ ὡρίσαντό τινες ὑγίειαν εἶναι τὴν εὐστάθειαν τῶν κατὰ φύσιν ἐνεργειῶν. Ὃ καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς κατὰ ψυχὴν εὐεξίας εἰπὼν, οὐχ ἁμαρτήσει τοῦ πρέποντος. Ὅθεν ὀρεκτικὴ τοῦ οἰκείου καὶ κατὰ φύσιν αὐτῇ ἀδιδάκτως ἐστὶν ἡ ψυχή. Διὸ ἐπαινετὴ πᾶσιν ἡ σωφροσύνη· καὶ ἀποδεκτὴ ἡ δικαιοσύνη· καὶ θαυμαστὴ ἡ ἀνδρεία· καὶ ἡ φρόνησις περισπούδαστος. Ἃ οἰκειότερά ἐστι τῇ ψυχῇ μᾶλλον, ἢ τῷ σώματι ἡ ὑγεία. Τὰ τέκνα, ἀγαπᾶτε τοὺς πατέρας. Οἱ γονεῖς, μὴ παροργίζετε τὰ τέκνα. Μὴ καὶ ἡ φύσις ταῦτα οὐ λέγει; Οὐδὲν καινὸν παραινεῖ Παῦλος, ἀλλὰ τὰ δεσμὰ τῆς φύσεως ἐπισφίγγει. Εἰ ἡ λέαινα στέργει τὰ ἐξ αὐτῆς, καὶ λύκος ὑπὲρ σκυλάκων μάχεται, τί εἴπῃ ἄνθρωπος καὶ τῆς ἐντολῆς παρακούων καὶ τὴν φύσιν παραχαράσσων, ὅταν ἢ παῖς ἀτιμάζῃ γῆρας πατρὸς, ἢ πατὴρ διὰ δευτέρων γάμων τῶν προτέρων παίδων ἐπιλανθάνηται; Ἀμήχανός ἐστιν ἡ στοργὴ τοῖς ἀλόγοις τέκνων καὶ γονέων πρὸς ἄλληλα, διότι ὁ δημιουργήσας αὐτὰ Θεὸς τὴν τοῦ λόγου ἔλλειψιν διὰ τῆς τῶν αἰσθητηρίων περιουσίας παρεμυθήσατο. Πόθεν γὰρ ἐν μυρίοις προβάτοις ἀρνειὸς τῶν σηκῶν ἐξαλλόμενος οἶδε μὲν τὴν χροίαν αὐτὴν καὶ τὴν φωνὴν τῆς μητρὸς, καὶ πρὸς αὐτὴν ἐπείγεται, ἐπιζητεῖ δὲ τὰς οἰκείας πηγὰς τοῦ γάλακτος; Κἂν πενιχραῖς ταῖς μητρῴαις περιτύχῃ θηλαῖς, ἐκείναις ἀρκεῖται, πολλὰ παραδραμὼν οὔθατα βαρυνόμενα. Καὶ ἡ μήτηρ ἐν μυρίοις ἄρνασιν ἐπιγινώσκει τὸ ἴδιον; Φωνὴ μία, χρόα ἡ αὐτὴ, ὀσμὴ παρὰ πάντων ὁμοία, ὅσον τῇ ἡμετέρᾳ ὀσφρήσει παρίσταται, ἀλλ' ὅμως ἐστί τις αὐτοῖς αἴσθησις τῆς ἡμετέρας καταλήψεως ὀξυτέρα, καθ' ἣν ἑκάστῳ πάρεστιν ἡ τοῦ οἰκείου διάγνωσις.
thought_title: Nature's untaught wisdom and the soul's natural virtues
orientation: Basil is drawing moral lessons from animal behavior, arguing that animals know by nature what preserves them, and now extends this to the soul's natural inclination toward virtue.
pass_a_gloss: For it cuts with its own claws the middle part of the fruits, so that they, if they sprout, might not become useless to it for food. And it dries these out, whenever it perceives them being soaked through; and it does not put them out at every season, but whenever it perceives beforehand that the air is being kept in a fair-weather condition. Certainly you would not see rain pouring down from clouds for as long a time as the grain has been put out by the ants. What speech could reach it? What hearing will contain it? What time will suffice to say and recount all the wonders of the craftsman? Let us also say with the prophet, How great have your works become, O Lord; all things in wisdom you made. Not therefore is it sufficient for us for a defense, that we were not taught by letters the things that are beneficial, since by the untaught law of nature we received the choice of what is profitable. Do you know what good you will do to your neighbor? What you wish to be done to yourself by another. Do you know what ever evil is? What you yourself would not choose to suffer from another. No root-cutting art, nor botanical experience discovered for the irrational animals the teaching of useful things, but naturally each of the animals is resourceful for its own safety, and possesses some inexpressible affinity toward what is according to nature. 9.4 And there are also among us the virtues according to nature, toward which the affinity of the soul exists not from teaching of humans, but from nature itself. For just as no word teaches us to hate disease, but we have automatically the aversion toward things that pain us; so also in the soul there is some untaught avoidance of evil. And every evil is a sickness of the soul, and virtue holds the place of health. For well did some define health to be the stability of the natural activities. And the one who says this also about the good condition of the soul will not miss what is fitting. Whence the soul is desirous of what is proper and according to nature for it, without teaching. Therefore temperance is praiseworthy to all; and justice is acceptable; and courage is admirable; and prudence is much sought after. These things are more proper to the soul than health is to the body. Children, love your fathers. Parents, do not provoke your children. Does not nature also say these things? Paul advises nothing new, but tightens the bonds of nature. If the lioness loves her own offspring, and the wolf fights for its whelps, what would a man say, both disobeying the commandment and falsifying nature, when either a child dishonors the old age of a father, or a father through second marriages forgets the former children? The mutual affection of children and parents toward each other is irresistible in the irrational animals, because the God who created them consoled the lack of reason through the abundance of the senses. For whence in ten thousand sheep does the lamb, leaping out from the folds, know the very color and the voice of its mother, and hurry toward her, and seek the proper springs of milk? And if it happens upon poor maternal teats, it is content with those, having run past many udders heavy with milk. And does the mother in ten thousand lambs recognize her own? One voice, the same color, a smell alike from all, as far as it presents itself to our sense of smell, but nevertheless there is in them some perception sharper than our comprehension, according to which the recognition of what is proper is present to each.

choices.why: Keeps the metaphor of bonds/ligaments that Basil uses to describe natural obligations; 'tightens' preserves the verb's force of making firmer what already exists.
The verb means to counterfeit or debase, as with coinage; 'falsifying' captures the moral corruption of nature Basil intends.
ἀμήχανος means 'against which no device can prevail'; 'irresistible' conveys the unstoppable force of natural affection Basil emphasizes.
λόγος here means rational capacity, not speech; 'lack of reason' is precise for Basil's contrast between animals and humans.
This Stoic technical term for natural appropriation is central to Basil's argument; 'affinity' preserves the sense of natural kinship and belonging.
εὐδινῇ is a rare adjective from εὔδιος meaning calm, clear weather; the rendering keeps the meteorological sense Basil intends for the ant's foresight.

pass_b_english: For it cuts through the very middle of the grains with its own claws, so that they will not sprout and become useless to it for food. And it dries them out whenever it perceives that they are soaked through. It does not bring them out at every season, but only when it perceives beforehand that the air is holding in a fair-weather condition. Indeed, you would not see rain pouring from the clouds for as long as the grain has been brought out by the ants. What speech could reach all this? What hearing could contain it? What time would be enough to tell and recount all the wonders of the Craftsman? Let us too say with the prophet, “How great are your works, O Lord; in wisdom you made them all” (Psalm 104:24, LXX Psalm 103:24). So it is not enough for our defense that we were not taught what is beneficial by letters, since we have received the choice of what is advantageous by the untaught law of nature. Do you know what good you will do to your neighbor? What you wish to have done to yourself by another. Do you know what evil is? What you yourself would not choose to suffer from another. No root-cutting skill and no botanical experience discovered the teaching of what is beneficial for the irrational animals. Rather, each of the animals is naturally resourceful for providing its own safety, and possesses a certain inexpressible affinity for what is according to nature. 9.4 There are also among us virtues according to nature, toward which the soul’s affinity exists not from human teaching but from nature itself. For just as no argument teaches us to hate sickness, but we have an automatic aversion to what causes pain, so too the soul has a certain untaught avoidance of evil. Every evil is a sickness of the soul, and virtue holds the place of health. For some have well defined health as the stability of the natural activities. If one says this also about the good condition of the soul, he will not miss what is fitting. From this the soul is, without teaching, desiring of what is its own and according to nature. Therefore temperance is praised by all, and justice is accepted, and courage is admired, and prudence is eagerly sought. These are more akin to the soul than health is to the body. Children, love your fathers. Parents, do not provoke your children. Does not nature itself say these things? Paul urges nothing new, but tightens the bonds of nature. If the lioness loves her offspring, and the wolf fights for its pups, what can a person say who both disobeys the commandment and falsifies nature, when either a child dishonors the old age of a father, or a father through a second marriage forgets his earlier children? The mutual affection of children and parents toward one another is irresistible in the irrational animals, because the God who created them compensated for the lack of reason through the abundance of their senses. For how is it that among countless sheep a lamb, leaping out from the folds, knows the very color and the voice of its mother, and hurries toward her, and seeks out its own fountains of milk? And if it happens upon its mother’s poor teats, it is content with those, having run past many heavy udders. And how does the mother among countless lambs recognize her own? The voice is one, the color the same, the smell alike from all, as far as it presents itself to our sense of smell—but nevertheless there is in them a perception sharper than our comprehension, by which each one has the recognition of its own.

last_rejected.source_quote: Ὡς ἐμεγαλύνθη τὰ ἔργα σου, Κύριε· πάντα ἐν σοφίᾳ ἐποίησας
last_rejected.why: The Greek quotes Psalm 103:24 LXX (Ὡς ἐμεγαλύνθη...), which corresponds to Hebrew Psalm 104:24. The citation reverses the numbering: should be 'Psalm 103:24 (LXX); Psalm 104:24 (Hebrew)'.
last_rejected.ruling: English gives both Hebrew and LXX numbers; order is a preference, not a major error. Reader is not misled.

last_rejected.quote: the grain has been brought out by the ants
last_rejected.source_quote: ἐκ τῶν μυρμήκων ὁ σῖτος προβέβληται
last_rejected.why: προβέβληται is middle/passive perfect: 'the grain has been brought out' misrepresents agency. The ants bring out the grain themselves (middle voice), not passive 'by the ants'.
last_rejected.fix: the ants have brought out the grain
last_rejected.ruling: προβέβληται is perfect middle/passive; 'brought out by the ants' correctly conveys the ants' action. No meaning lost.
